Hyderabad Police arrest four for using aluminium foil disguised as silver foil in sweets, paan and bakery products
 Aluminium-coated sugar balls were used by bakeries for cake decoration, said Hyderabad Police Commissioner Mahesh Bhagwat. The police demonstrated two preliminary methods to distinguish fake aluminium varaq from genuine silver foil
 Updated - November 17, 2026 07:49 pm IST - HYDERABAD 
 The Hindu Bureau READ LATER 
 SEE ALL 
 Remove 
 Hyderabad Police Commissioner Mahesh Bhagwat and other police officers checking the aluminium foils which were used disguised as fake silver foil (waraq) in sweets and other products, in Hyderabad on Tuesday (November 17, 2026).
 | Photo Credit: SIDDHANT THAKUR
 The Hyderabad City Police have busted four illegal manufacturing units involved in producing and supplying aluminium foil and flakes disguised as edible silver waraq, arresting four persons and seizing large quantities of counterfeit material, adulterants and manufacturing equipment, posing a potential health risk to consumers. 
 Announcing the arrests at a press conference at the Telangana Integrated Command and Control Centre (TGICCC) in Banjara Hills, Hyderabad, on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), Hyderabad Police Commissioner Mahesh M. Bhagwat said that the Commissioner’s Task Force, along with local police personnel, conducted raids at four manufacturing units in the Charminar and Falaknuma areas. Four separate cases were registered against the units for manufacturing and selling fake edible silver waraq and silver flakes in violation of food safety standards.
 Hyderabad City Police display the seized aluminium foils disguised as waraqs used in sweets and other food products at Telangana Integrated Command and Control Centre in Hyderabad on Tuesday (November 17, 2026).
 | Photo Credit: 
 SIDDHANT THAKUR
 Who were arrested?
 The accused have been identified as Mohammed Akber (45), owner of Ittehad Waraq Shop near Mecca Masjid and Charminar Bus Stand, Mohammed Wali Uddin (62), owner of UTC Silver Leafs at Punch Mohalla near Charminar New Bus Stand, Mohammed Shareef (60), owner of M.A. Metro Waraq Shop opposite Charminar Bus Stop, and Mohammed Jaleel Khan (47), owner of Tara Unit at Achi Reddy Nagar, Bibikachasma, Falaknuma.
 What was seized?
 During the raids, police seized 49 bundles of fake silver foil made of aluminium, including 41 bundles measuring 14 cm × 10 cm and eight smaller bundles measuring 7 cm × 8 cm. They also seized 10 kg of aluminium flakes packed in 10 cartons, two polythene bags containing silver flakes weighing 1 kg each, and 32 covers of flakes weighing 50 grams each.
 The other seized material included 1 kg of fake silver-coated sugar balls, 30 jars of Qiwam weighing 500 grams each, three tubs containing approximately 30 kg of Qiwam, 20 bottles of Qiwam weighing 500 grams each, two gunny bags of tobacco weighing 25 kg each, 1 kg of talcum powder, 50 bottles of flavoured paan chutney, five books of animal skin sheets, around 10 litres of glucose and approximately 40 kg of maize starch.
 Manufacturing equipment, including a mixer grinder, a long mixer, a packing machine, a weighing machine, an LPG cylinder, a gas stove and a cooking utensil, was also seized.
 Fake varaq supplied for use in kaju katli, kaju rolls, cham cham and sweet paan
 According to the police, the accused were manufacturing aluminium waraq in place of genuine silver foil and supplying it to sweet manufacturers for use in products such as Kaju Katli, Kaju Rolls, Cham Cham and sweet paan. They were also manufacturing aluminium-coated sugar balls and supplying them to bakeries for use as cake decorations and toppings.
 Aluminium flakes procured from Uttar Pradesh
 The accused were allegedly procuring aluminium flakes from Uttar Pradesh and using them instead of genuine silver flakes in Zarda, Qiwam and other flavoured paan preparations. The police said the units were operating without valid licences from the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI).
 By falsely marketing the aluminium-based products as genuine silver, the accused were making monetary gains and had established a supply network catering to local and reputed sweet shops, bakeries and paan outlets across Telangana. They were also procuring larger quantities from other States during peak festival seasons to meet increased demand, police said.
 Mr. Bhagwat said the practice amounted to cheating consumers while also posing potential health risks. Consumption of non-food-grade aluminium products over a prolonged period could lead to kidney damage, neurological effects, bone disorders and digestive irritation, besides excessive accumulation of aluminium in the body.
 Hyderabad Police Commissioner Mahesh Bhagwat and other police officers showed how aluminium foils can be detected at a press conference in Hyderabad on Tuesday (November 17, 2026).
 | Photo Credit: 
 SIDDHANT THAKUR
 Police demonstrate tests to identify fake silver
 The police demonstrated two preliminary methods to distinguish fake aluminium waraq from genuine silver foil.
 In the dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl) test, aluminium reacts with the acid, producing hydrogen gas and gradually dissolving, while genuine silver normally does not react with dilute HCl.
 Rubbing test
 In the rubbing test, genuine silver foil generally breaks down into very fine particles when gently rubbed, whereas aluminium foil may crumple, tear or form small ball-like pieces. The police clarified that these were only preliminary screening methods and laboratory analysis was necessary for confirmation. The chemical test should be handled only by trained personnel, as the hydrogen gas produced is flammable.
 Cases were registered at Charminar Police Station, Hussaini Alam police station, Moghalpura police station and Falaknuma police station under Sections 318(4) and 110 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). Mr. Bhagwat said the practice also violated Regulation 2.11.4 of the Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011.
